evaluation.positioning_hook: A self-doubting teen girl in a quiet Midwest town discovers she can copy anyone she touches, then gets trapped between a biotech cover-up, a missing billionaire, and the life she was never supposed to have.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is immediately legible and commercially legible: a teen discovery story wrapped in a conspiracy chase, with body-swap mechanics that are easy to sell in a trailer. The audience is narrower than a four-quadrant event because the script leans hard into identity, family, and moral panic rather than pure spectacle.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands almost immediately in the opening chase and then sharpens with the reveal that the girl can shapeshift by touch. The script keeps clarifying the engine through Ava/Madison, the foam, and the Eric Huntington cover-up, so the premise is easy to explain in two sentences.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Ava/Madison is a strong lead because the script builds her from insecurity, moral instinct, and a real hunger to be seen, then complicates her with identity confusion and power. June, Shannon, Priscilla, and David all have distinct voices and playable contradictions, which gives the movie more than one memorable face.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script takes a familiar teen-conspiracy setup and makes the body-swap rules the emotional and thematic center, not just a gimmick. The choice to let identity literally migrate through touch, memory, and class resentment gives the material a sharper, stranger edge than standard genre fare.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The first act is built like a chase, then the story keeps escalating through school, mall, lab, and warehouse reversals without losing the central question of who Ava really is. The back half is especially propulsive once the script starts weaponizing the identity swaps in pursuit scenes and confrontations.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea feels fresh because the shapeshifting is tied to memory, self-worth, and social class rather than just disguise. The Ava/Madison reversal and the final emotional handoff between the two girls make the concept feel surprising but inevitable.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The small-town setting has useful texture: burger joint, school, mall, ranch house, forest road, and a hidden lab all feel story-generating. The world becomes more specific once the company’s security apparatus, disinformation, and local buyouts are introduced, though the movie still functions primarily as a contained genre container.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a distinct blend of teen awkwardness, paranoid sci-fi, and emotional sincerity. It can jump from joke-y high school banter to body-horror mutation to earnest found-family sentiment without feeling random.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Under the chase mechanics, the script is really about class shame, parental love, self-hatred, and the seduction of power. The Ava/Madison identity confusion and the David relationship suggest a deeper psychological layer that rewards a second look.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The movie is anchored by Ava and June, with Shannon as a strong friend dynamic and Priscilla/David/Wolcott as a vivid antagonistic system. It is not an ensemble in the broad sense, but the relationships do generate recurring friction and payoff.

lead_characters.name: Ava
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 16, high-school student, white, working-class suburban/small-town background.
lead_characters.hook: Ava is the script’s emotional center: bright, self-conscious, funny when she’s cornered, and quietly furious that the world seems to hand other girls the life she thinks she should have. She starts as a teen with a crush and a chip on her shoulder, then becomes the person who can see through the company’s lies because she’s the one person in town who still believes morality matters.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Saoirse Ronan in Lady Bird or Kaitlyn Dever in Short Term 12 — a role that lives on interior contradiction, wounded intelligence, and the ability to make self-doubt feel cinematic.

lead_characters.name: June
lead_characters.hook: June is a hard-edged, funny, overextended mom who looks like she’s improvising adulthood in real time, but she turns out to be tougher and more capable than anyone in the room. The script gives her real bite, real love for Ava, and a late-breaking physical competence that makes her more than a parent function.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role Frances McDormand or Allison Janney can turn into a full-body performance — sharp comic timing, lived-in exhaustion, and a late-act reveal of steel.

lead_characters.name: Shannon
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 16, high-school student, teen friend, plus-size, curly-haired.
lead_characters.hook: Shannon is the loyal best friend with a grounded, practical voice and enough social confidence to keep Ava from disappearing into her own head. She’s not just comic relief; she’s the person who keeps the movie tethered to ordinary teenage life while the plot goes fully off the rails.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of best-friend role that gives an actor the same kind of scene-stealing lift as Beanie Feldstein in Lady Bird — warmth, timing, and the chance to be the audience’s anchor.

lead_characters.name: Priscilla
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late 40s, security executive, corporate, hard-edged.
lead_characters.hook: Priscilla is the polished face of the operation: controlled, unsentimental, and smart enough to sound reasonable while she’s doing something monstrous. She’s one of the script’s best antagonistic presences because she can pivot from corporate calm to threat in a single line.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is prestige-villain territory like Patricia Clarkson in Sharp Objects or Carrie Coon in Gone Girl — a role that lets an actor weaponize intelligence, restraint, and moral vacancy.

lead_characters.name: David
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 90s body / adult male consciousness, shapeshifter, mentally fragmented.
lead_characters.hook: David is tragic, unstable, and strangely tender: a damaged survivor whose need for connection curdles into manipulation and violence. The script gives him a heartbreaking split between vulnerability and menace, especially once his identity starts fracturing under the pressure of the touch-based copying.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the same volatile showcase as Paul Dano in Prisoners or Michael Shannon in Take Shelter — emotional instability, pathos, and real danger in the same performance.

lead_characters.name: Wolcott
lead_characters.hook: Wolcott is the cold technocrat who treats human beings like prototypes and sees suffering as a tolerable cost of progress. He’s less flashy than Priscilla, but he gives the movie its institutional evil and its most chillingly clinical dialogue.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of polished, icy authority role that lets an actor play the same unnerving control as Bryan Cranston in Drive or Michael Keaton in Spotlight — intelligence with a moral void underneath.

lead_characters.name: Jamieson
lead_characters.hook: Jamieson is the blunt instrument of the operation: disciplined, intimidating, and always one step away from violence. He’s not deep, but he’s useful, readable, and gives the chase scenes a credible human threat.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a solid character-actor enforcer role in the vein of Shea Whigham or David Harbour — physical authority, dry menace, and a chance to make a small role memorable.

lead_characters.name: Mills
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 20s, security operative, ex-military, father.
lead_characters.hook: Mills is the most conflicted of the security men, and the script smartly lets him carry guilt without turning him into a full convert. He’s the one who hints that the machine is staffed by people who know they’re doing wrong but keep going anyway.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of morally split supporting role that gives an actor the same appeal as Ben Foster in Hell or High Water — contained intensity, suppressed conscience, and a late-act pivot.

lead_characters.name: Wilma
lead_characters.hook: Wilma is the humane face of a brutal system, which makes her both useful and tragic. She’s the character who helps explain the rules while also showing how the company recruits ordinary people into extraordinary harm.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a strong supporting role for an actor who can play empathy under pressure, in the lane of Jurnee Smollett in Lovecraft Country or Merritt Wever in Godless.

casting_characteristics: teen lead with strong emotional range
supporting roles with age-flexible authority casting

technical.vfx_details: Body transformation work, skin bubbling/mutation, identity swaps, and a few stylized chase beats; mostly practical performance-driven with selective digital augmentation.
technical.sfx_needs: Foam spray effects, burns/mutation makeup, fire/smoke, cattle prods, gunfire, vehicle chase beats, sprinkler/fire sequence.

rights_flags.detail: Eric Huntington is a fictional character, but the script references the New York Times, CNN, and a billionaire tech mogul in a way that stays fictionalized.
TikTok, Trader Joe’s, Honda Civic, Beretta APX Carry, iPhone, and Purina are named on the page.
Indiana Jones is referenced by title in dialogue.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: streamer-first or specialty theatrical with genre marketing and strong trailer hook.

budget.note: Contemporary locations keep the spend contained, but the transformation effects, night chase material, fire/foam sequence, and multiple company vehicles push this above a simple indie container.

casting.note: The lead has to carry teen vulnerability, action, body-horror reactions, and a late-film identity split; the supporting villain track also needs actors who can play corporate calm and threat without flattening.

development.note: The premise is clear, but the Ava/Madison identity reveal and the late emotional handoff are the kind of structural turns that will be closely scrutinized in development.

comp_set.title: Freaky
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the body-swap identity engine and the fun of watching a character discover power through an unstable new self.

comp_set.title: The Faculty
comp_set.why_it_comps: Small-town teen paranoia, secret invasion, and a school/community under covert control make this a close tonal and structural neighbor.

comp_set.title: Chronicle
comp_set.why_it_comps: Teen discovery of extraordinary power inside a grounded contemporary world, with the emotional cost of becoming something else.

comp_set.title: The Craft
comp_set.why_it_comps: Teen identity, social hierarchy, and power-as-self-reinvention all sit in the same lane, even though the mechanics are different.

comp_set.title: Upgrade
comp_set.why_it_comps: The script has the same efficient genre propulsion and body-control anxiety, with a contained production footprint and a strong hook.

audience_target.primary_audience: Genre audiences who like smart, emotional sci-fi thrillers with a teen lead and a strong identity hook.
audience_target.demographics: Skews 16-34 with a female tilt; also plays to older genre fans who respond to body-horror, conspiracy, and found-family dynamics.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary small-town locations, a limited cast, and selective transformation effects keep this in indie territory, though the chase/fire sequences and creature makeup require disciplined scope.

types_of_buyers: producer-directors looking for a contained breakout feature
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of smart, character-forward genre movies that can sell on premise but land on emotion. The script’s mix of teen identity, body horror, and conspiracy makes it attractive to buyers looking for a distinctive but producible hook.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature; the Ava/Madison story resolves cleanly and the supporting characters do not suggest a separate franchise vector.

strengths.what_it_means: A buyer can understand the movie in one breath, which is a real advantage in a crowded genre market. That makes it easy to package for streamer development, specialty financing, or a director looking for a clean breakout premise.
strengths.evidence: The opening chase, the shapeshift reveal, and the later explanation that touch copies memories and identity all arrive early and clearly.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Ava is a strong emotional engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The role gives the movie a real center of gravity, which is what turns a high-concept genre piece into a star vehicle. That is the kind of part that attracts young prestige actors who want vulnerability, wit, and escalation in one package.
strengths.evidence: Her insecurity about her body, her crush on Liam, her instinct to help the little girl, and her refusal to become the company’s tool all define her.

strengths.what_it_means: The mechanics are not just gimmick; they create chase logic, emotional reversals, and a built-in visual language for identity conflict. That gives the script repeatable set pieces without needing to inflate the world into something expensive.
strengths.evidence: Touching copies memories, foam blocks and distorts the process, and the characters keep changing bodies to hide, escape, or manipulate.

strengths.what_it_means: The burger joint, school, locker room, mall, and friend-group banter give the movie a recognizable social texture that broadens the appeal beyond pure sci-fi fans. That helps the script play as both a genre ride and a coming-of-age story.
strengths.evidence: Ava and Shannon’s banter, the Liam/Christy triangle, and the school scenes all feel specific rather than generic.

strengths.what_it_means: Priscilla, Wolcott, Jamieson, Mills, and Wilma create a believable corporate-security machine, which gives the movie more than one face of threat. That makes the project easier to cast and market because the villainy is distributed across memorable roles.
strengths.evidence: Priscilla’s school confrontation, Wolcott’s lab scenes, and the security team’s escalating pursuit all show a coherent operation.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ending lands on emotional recognition.
strengths.what_it_means: The final Ava/Madison exchange gives the movie a human payoff that can stick with audiences after the genre mechanics are over. That kind of ending helps word-of-mouth because it resolves the concept through feeling, not just plot.
strengths.evidence: Real Ava recognizing Madison by the pendant and telling her, “I know who you are,” is the movie’s emotional thesis in one beat.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, high-concept sci-fi thriller with a real star-making lead role and a contained production footprint that keeps the buy in a reachable indie lane. The script’s strongest commercial asset is that it turns a body-swap premise into an emotional identity story, which gives buyers both a trailer hook and a reason to care.

items.area: The Ava/Madison reveal is a big swing.
items.detail: The late identity reversal is the script’s sharpest structural bet, because the audience has spent most of the movie tracking Ava as the protagonist. That can be a thrilling reframe, but it is also the point where buyers will ask how cleanly the emotional contract survives the switch.

items.area: The body-swap rules get dense fast.
items.detail: Touch, memory transfer, foam exposure, body retention, and identity bleed all have to stay legible while the plot is moving at speed. The script mostly manages it, but the mechanics are complex enough that a producer will flag clarity as a development pressure point.

items.area: The third act leans hard on effects and fire.
items.detail: The secret-lab climax adds foam ignition, mutation makeup, body burns, and a lab-wide fire sequence, which is the most expensive stretch of the movie. That is still producible, but it is the section most likely to push scope if the budget gets squeezed.

The actor playing Ava has to sell teen insecurity, action, body-horror, comic timing, and a late-film identity fracture. That is a real showcase, but it also narrows the pool to performers who can carry both the emotional and physical load.

items.area: The corporate conspiracy is familiar terrain.
items.detail: Secret lab, private security, billionaire biotech, and town-wide cover-up are all effective, but they live in a well-traveled genre lane. The script’s freshness comes from the identity mechanic, so the surrounding conspiracy has to stay lean and not over-explain itself.

issues.headline: The biggest conversation is the late identity reversal, because that is where the movie either becomes memorable or risks feeling like a conceptual trick. Beyond that, the main friction is practical: the effects-heavy climax and the demanding lead role are both real asks, even inside an otherwise contained indie package.
